title: Paradise Lost
author: John Milton
openingText: Of Man's First Disobedience, and the Fruit Of that Forbidden Tree, whose mortal taste Brought Death into the World, and all our woe, With loss of Eden, till one greater Man Restore us, and regain the blissful Seat, Sing Heav'nly Muse, that on the secret top Of Oreb, or of Sinai, didst inspire That Shepherd, who first taught the chosen Seed.
about:
Paradise Lost is a 12-book epic poem in blank verse, telling the story of the fall of man — Satan's rebellion, the creation of Adam and Eve, the temptation in Eden, and the expulsion. Milton draws on Genesis and on classical epic to create what is probably the most ambitious poem in English. It is also the strangest: Satan is the most charismatic character, and the poem cannot quite resolve whether to admire him.

John Milton wrote Paradise Lost in his fifties and sixties, after he had gone blind. He dictated it to his daughters and assistants. It was published in 1667. The poem set the standard for what English-language epic could be and shaped almost every long English poem that came after.

angleCards.title: Satan as the most compelling character.
angleCards.text: Many readers come away feeling Satan is the real hero of this poem. I want to understand whether Milton intended that, or whether the poem got away from him — and what it means if it did.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Paradise Lost to understand whether Satan is the real hero — whether Milton intended him to be compelling, or whether the poem got away from him and made the villain more interesting than God.

angleCards.title: The free will problem.
angleCards.text: God knew Adam would fall before he created him. So what does it mean that Adam freely chose it? Milton thought this was the central theological puzzle, and he wrote twelve books trying to answer it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Paradise Lost to think about the free will problem — God knew Adam would fall, so what does it mean that Adam chose it? I want to follow Milton's argument about divine foreknowledge and human freedom.

angleCards.title: What Milton thought he was doing.
angleCards.text: Milton announced his intention as "justifying the ways of God to men." I want to track whether the poem achieves that — or whether it ends up somewhere more complicated and more honest.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Paradise Lost to understand what Milton thought he was doing — justifying the ways of God to man — versus what he actually did, which may be something more ambiguous and more interesting.

angleCards.title: The politics in the poem.
angleCards.text: Milton lived through the English Civil War, helped justify regicide, and watched the Restoration bring back monarchy. What he put into Satan — and into the Court of Heaven — is not accidental.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Paradise Lost to understand the politics embedded in it — Milton was a Parliamentarian who lived through the execution of a king and the Restoration. I want to find what he put into Satan and into the celestial monarchy.

cast.name: Satan
cast.description: Starts in heaven as the greatest of the angels. Falls to Hell, refuses to repent, and decides that if he cannot destroy God he will corrupt God's new creation instead. The most vivid character in the poem.

cast.name: God
cast.description: Foreknows everything, including the Fall. Permits it because forced virtue is not virtue. His speeches are the most difficult part of the poem — deliberately so.

cast.name: Adam
cast.description: Created perfect, warned clearly, given every reason to obey. Eats the fruit anyway, after Eve, knowing exactly what he is doing. His choice is the poem's central act.

cast.name: Eve
cast.description: Persuaded by Satan in the form of a serpent. Goes alone into the garden against Raphael's warning. The most psychologically complex character in the poem.

cast.name: Raphael
cast.description: Sent by God to warn Adam. Tells him the story of Satan's rebellion and fall in Books 5–8. The poem's internal storyteller — through him Milton narrates the war in heaven.

cast.name: Sin & Death
cast.description: Allegorical figures born from Satan's rebellion — Sin from his mind, Death from their union. They build the bridge from Hell to Earth once the Fall is accomplished. Milton's darkest invention.

acclaim.quote: The reason Milton wrote in fetters when he wrote of Angels & God, and at liberty when of Devils & Hell, is because he was a true Poet and of the Devil's party without knowing it.
acclaim.context: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, 1790

whyItMatters.title: Satan as a Charismatic Argument
whyItMatters.body: The first books of Paradise Lost give Satan some of the most powerful speeches in English poetry. He is proud, defiant, self-aware. Blake said Milton was "of the Devil's party without knowing it." The poem argues a theology and undermines it in the same lines.

whyItMatters.title: Justifying the Ways of God
whyItMatters.body: Milton's stated aim is to "justify the ways of God to men" — to make sense of why God allowed the fall, why suffering exists. He attempts the hardest theological problem head-on. Whether he succeeds is what readers have argued about for three hundred years.

whyItMatters.title: The English Epic
whyItMatters.body: Before Milton, English poetry had no epic to match Homer or Virgil. Paradise Lost was the answer. The blank verse, the syntax, the diction set a standard that subsequent English poetry could either follow or react against. Both options created modern English literature.
